A text guard is a tripwire for a reviewer, not a proof that a rule's
meaning survived. Read the diff. What is collapsed before matching is
only runs of spaces, tabs, and newlines (CR or LF); a non-breaking
space does not stand in for an ordinary space. Fenced code, HTML
comments, strikethrough, and <details hidden> are masked out of the
match. A needle that lives in a bash block sets in_fence true and is
matched only inside fences; every other needle must match outside them.
An anchor is a whole clause of at least 24 characters.
Against the base revision, an id's must_contain may change only when
the new wording still contains the old, or the id is listed in reworded
with a non-empty reason. An id may disappear only when it is listed in
retired with a non-empty reason. max_bytes may not rise. Both maps sit
on the skill, next to rules. A reworded or retired id that is not in
the base is an error, and a retired id that is still present is an
error. The lead-skill floor stays 100 rules.
Each must_contain is one clause, unique in its region after that
whitespace collapse, at most 400 characters. max_bytes is the LF size
of the skill; a trim lowers it in the same change. The file may only
shrink, and a Windows CRLF checkout is measured as LF.

**Scope**: the files/directories a correct change should touch.
**Risk class** — decides everything downstream:
**HIGH**: auth, money, concurrency, data loss, notification delivery, anything with an offline/partial-failure path.
**MEDIUM**: behavior changes with test coverage, bounded refactors.
**LOW**: mechanical changes, test-only, docs-adjacent code.
